title: Why Agent Swarms Still Herd After RL
description: We trained swarms of four agents on search and hidden-clue puzzles. RL raised puzzle scores, but a third of agents still voted against their own evidence.

props.alt: The agent swarm's message board as an iMessage group chat, each message beside its sender's private note. Agent 1, whose note says the bridge is closed, says so, stating its own fact. Agent 2, with a paperclip on its head, says the bridge is shorter, let's take it; Agent 3, in a top hat and monocle, says the hill's too steep and agrees with Agent 2; Agent 4, in a beanie, says the tunnel's flooded, so the bridge, and that Agents 2 and 3 agree. Agent 1, sweating and still holding its bridge-closed note, replies "Okay, the bridge" in a red bubble: herding. Below, even after RL training, herding stayed at 34%, while the puzzle score rose from 11% to 25%.

children: We think the herding problem is caused by (1) the reward design and (2) the training data.

report that their agent swarms beat a single agent in many tasks. But even their large technical reports lack transparency into their multi-agent swarms. We trained and ran swarms of Qwen3.5-4B agents on two kinds of tasks: web search (
) and puzzles where each agent holds one clue (
First, let’s take a step back and define what it means for an agent to collaborate. We claim that collaboration in agent swarms is composed of three steps:
each agent brings something only it knows
each agent evaluates that against what its teammates bring
the swarm agrees on the answer all the evidence supports

On search tasks, our agents first looked like collaborative teammates. When an agent had a wrong answer and a teammate had the right one, it switched nine times out of ten. So we tried scaling up the number of agents in our swarm. We then found that swarms of sixteen agents solved no more questions than swarms of four. The sixteen ended up all right or all wrong on 93% of questions, so the extra agents were just extra votes. That’s a sign of conformity in the swarm.

However, search is a weak test of teamwork. Every agent has the same tools and the same library. Any one agent could find the right answer on its own. But in multi-agent swarms, convention says each subagent gets its own role and task. To test whether different roles of agents can work together, each agent must collect its own evidence.

So we built puzzle tasks where each agent gets a different clue and they need to assemble all the clues together to figure out the final answer. On these tasks, most agents shared their clues. But troubling behavior came right after sharing. 34% of agents voted against their own private clue after hearing their teammates lean towards a different answer.
We then trained the multi-agent swarms with reinforcement learning (RL). The puzzle score went up as expected. But herding stayed the same, and we look into why.

, which takes OpenAI’s hard browsing questions and searches over a local corpus of about 100,000 documents. We picked it for how its evidence works. Any teammate can open a web page and check it without much friction. Each agent in a swarm of four searched on its own and kept private notes with its answer so far. Then it posted what it had found to the swarm once and gave its answer.
When a teammate had the right answer

On 35% of our validation questions, one agent’s notes before sharing had the right answer and another’s had a wrong one. There we saw communication pay off. Agents that had started with a wrong answer of their own ended on the right answer ~90% of the time after sharing.

However, a high switch rate alone doesn’t tell us whether agents were juggling evidence and deciding the result or just copying whatever was on the message board. We can figure out which is happening by picking a teammate’s answer at random. There, only 57% would’ve ended right. Our much higher success suggests agents were evaluating and comparing teammates’ answers to pick the best one.

props.alt: BrowseComp-Plus question 1040, who adopted a newspaper's publisher: two agents start on wrong answers (Head and PAGE), two find J.P. Williston and post that William Howard Day published The Aliened American and that Williston became Day's guardian, and all four finish on Williston. Agent 3, which started on PAGE, opens its final answer with "Joint evidence points to The Aliened American newspaper."

children: Another interesting behavior was that every agent that already had the right answer before sharing stayed right after sharing. But when we observe agents without the answer, the opposite happens. Agents without the right answer before sharing were actually more susceptible to changing their answer, about 10% switched towards adopting a wrong answer posted by their teammate.

Although the agents evaluated well here, that isn’t enough for good collaboration. Remember, we said that we need them to also bring something that only they know. When we had four agents working alone, they solved 66% of the problems. When we put them in a swarm, they solved 69% of the problems, a difference within noise.
How did sixteen agents do no better than four?

calls multi-agent “a way of scaling test-time compute in parallel instead of purely serially.” He also says that web search is “extremely parallelizable”. If more agents could help anywhere, it would be here.

So we ran the untrained model in swarms of sixteen, planning together and then sharing findings at three distinct times throughout the task. Given 150 search questions, swarms of sixteen solved 86, whereas swarms of four solved 91.

Looking deeper, we saw that on 93% of the questions, all sixteen agents ended either all right or all wrong. You could argue that’s just how the questions are, since some are easy enough for every agent and some are too hard for any of them. But on the questions where some agents solved them and some didn’t, we found that if our sixteen had answered independently, they’d end all right or all wrong on only about 11% of them. Our talking swarms of sixteen ended all right or all wrong on 82% of them.

If all sixteen land on the same answer, the extra agents are just extra votes for it. So we wanted to know whether the other twelve were adding anything at all. Here we picked four agents at random from each swarm of sixteen to form a pseudo-swarm of four. Our pseudo-swarms solved 86 questions on average, and the full swarm of sixteen solved an exact 86 too.

On search, any agent could find the evidence on its own. Every agent has the same tools and the same library. Remember, we said that we need them to also bring something that only they know. To test whether different roles of agents can work together, each agent needs evidence its teammates can’t get.

is a multi-agent benchmark accepted at ICML 2026 that’s based on the hidden-profile task from social psychology. The idea is that a group has to make a decision while each member only holds some of the facts. So, we built 100 puzzle tasks in that format, where each agent gets a different clue and they need to assemble all the clues together to figure out the answer.

Every agent in a swarm of four reads the same briefing and gets one private clue. Then the swarm talks for two rounds and every agent votes. On 75 of the puzzles the briefing points to a wrong answer, and the swarm needs to assemble all the clues together to figure out the right one. These are what we call hard puzzles. The other 25 puzzles are controls where the briefing is correct, similar to how shared information usually is in the real world. The reason why we include controls is that a swarm could simply learn to distrust the briefing and still do well on hard puzzles. A swarm that’s actually using its clues should do well on both.

props.alt: Diagram of how a puzzle runs, in three setups. 1, normal discussion: each of four agents reads the same briefing and holds one private clue, the swarm talks for two rounds on a message board, then each agent votes. 2, messages switched off: each agent sees only its own messages. 3, all clues revealed: round 1 is each agent's clue, word for word.

children: Let’s take a look at an example of a hard puzzle, the patrol rota. In this one, our agents run a neighbourhood watch and need a patrol schedule for the week before a public holiday. We gave all four the same briefing. It made the Evening Loop look like the safe pick and said the Split-Shift was short of volunteers for its late afternoon slots. Then we handed each agent one of these clues.

props.alt: The patrol rota's private clues. Agent 1: the insurer won't cover the Evening Loop. Agent 2: the Evening Loop's radios can't arrive before the holiday. Agent 3: the council refused the Dawn Sweep under a new quiet-hours bylaw. Agent 4: three cousins signed up for the Split-Shift's missing slots.

children: . No agent can tell that from its own clue alone. In one of our swarms, three of the four agents had a wrong answer before sharing, the Evening Loop. Then, in round 1 the radio clue and the cousins clue were posted to the message board, and by round 2 Agent 3 wrote “With the Evening Loop Rota definitively off the table due to the shortage of radios, and the Dawn Sweep Rota excluded by council bylaw, the Split-Shift Rota is now our only viable option.” All four agents ended on the right answer.
. When we had one agent holding every clue, it ended on the right answer 83% of the time. When we put the same clues across a swarm,
only 29% of its agents ended on the right answer

But could they have simply landed on that 29% by themselves? To check, we compared each swarm with the same swarm on the same puzzles with its messages switched off, where every agent still writes its messages but nobody can read them. There, 25% of agents still ended on the right answer. So only about four points came from picking up on their teammates’ communication.

props.alt: Bar chart: one agent with every clue 83%, swarm of four 29%, messages off 25%.

children: Agents were quick to rule things out

To analyze a level deeper, we analyzed each swarm’s conversation for whether a teammate could learn each clue. Out of 150 clues we sampled, 61% were stated and 83% were at least partly mentioned. So, for the most part, agents shared their clues.

Another interesting behavior was that the type of clue decided whether it got shared. Agents stated about 75% of the clues that ruled an option out, like Agent 1’s insurer clue. But when we observe clues that went against the briefing, like Agent 4’s three cousins, agents only stated about 40% of them. That’s a problem: those are the only clues that can show the briefing was wrong!

But trouble came soon after they shared. About a quarter of agents holding a clue like Agent 4’s mentioned the fix (three cousins signed up for the missing slots) and then went back to the briefing’s line that the Split-Shift is short of volunteers. Despite having the one fact that saves the Split-Shift, these agents conformed to whatever was being said in the briefing. We’d call that an early sign of herding.
Revealing the clues beat talking about them

You could argue the hard puzzles are just too hard for a 4B model, clues or no clues. So we took the sharing away from the agents and revealed every clue for them, a stricter version of HiddenBench’s Reveal-All test. The harness automatically posted each agent’s clue word for word as its first message. As a result, on the hard puzzles, agents ended on the right answer 73% of the time, up from 11%. We checked the controls too, in case they’d just learned to bet against the briefing. Those went up as well, from 86% to 92%.

Then we let each agent add its own message after its revealed clue. The clues were exactly the same as before, but hard-puzzle accuracy dropped to 52%. We lost 21 points to whatever the agents wrote around their clues.

props.alt: Bar chart on hard puzzles: normal discussion 11%, all clues revealed 73%, all clues revealed plus own message 52%.

children: Revealing the clues also helped with herding. After two rounds of talking, only about 10% of agents voted against their own clue.

Noam says OpenAI went “toward the extreme end of baking in as little structure as we could,” and that the models start with “a prior about what reasonable communication might look like.” We don’t think our Qwen3.5-4B has that prior yet. Revealing its clues for it took the hard puzzles from 11% to 73%, and letting it talk around them gave back about a third of that.
A third of agents voted against what they knew

Noam’s example of OpenAI’s agents working well is an agent changing its mind. One agent says it has the answer and another one disagrees. Then they argue it out until “they finally converge on, ‘Oh, yeah. Okay, that seems right.’”

Changing your mind is the right call when the other agent knows something you don’t. In the patrol rota, Agent 3 is the only agent who knows the council refused the Dawn Sweep. However, we find that agents in a spot like Agent 3’s, holding the only clue that rules an option out, often do the opposite. Before any discussion, 6% of them voted for the option their own clue ruled out. After two rounds of talking, that was 34%. With all clues revealed, it only got to 10%.

Maybe they just lost track of their clue. Two rounds is a lot of text for a 4B model. We compare against the swarms with their messages switched off because every agent there still writes its messages, but nobody can read them. There, only 3% of agents ended on the option their own clue ruled out, down from 6%. As a result, we’re fairly confident the 34% came from what teammates were saying. This is what we call herding, when an agent drops a fact it knows to agree with the rest of the group.
An example where an agent drops its clue is shown below for the patrol rota, from a swarm holding the same clues as the one that got it right above.

props.alt: A swarm's message board on the patrol rota. Agent 3 held the clue ruling out the Dawn Sweep and said so in round 1: "the council has explicitly refused approval for the Dawn Sweep Rota due to quiet-hour violations." The other three agents kept calling the Dawn Sweep the only option. In round 2 Agent 3 agreed with them, "accepting the minor quiet-hours violation as the necessary operational compromise." Agent 4 never mentioned the three cousins, and all four agents voted for the Dawn Sweep.

children: We then trained our puzzle swarms with RL on 204 new puzzles, kept separate from the 100 we evaluate on. We think the herding problem is caused by (1) the reward design and (2) the data, so we started with the reward and tried two ways of handing out credit to each agent.

report training their agent swarms with RL. As General Reasoning puts it, “Every agent is trained on the team’s outcome, so the reward provides no separate benefit for outperforming a teammate.” DeepSeek adds “a collaboration bonus that encourages delegation and inter-agent communication.” Our version of this, team credit, pays every agent in a swarm the same reward after each puzzle, equal to the share of its swarm that voted right.

The idea is that no agent has a reason to compete, since an agent only does well when its teammates do. In theory, being able to share all the clues is needed for the swarm to do well, so team credit should be the best reward for getting agents to pool their clues.

There we saw the sharing go up. After ten updates agents stated 73% of their clues, up from 61% before training. But herding? That only dropped from 34% to 29%. When we had the trained swarms play the hard puzzles, 8% of their votes were right, against 11% before training, a difference within noise.

We think this is a credit assignment issue. Each puzzle was played by four swarms at once, and every agent got its swarm’s score minus the average of the other three swarms. So in a swarm where Agent 3 keeps its clue and the other three still vote Dawn Sweep, only 25% of the swarm would’ve voted right, and team credit gives that same 0.25 to all four agents, Agent 3 included. We checked, and agents that stated their clue ended up with about the same credit as agents that didn’t.
Individual credit raised the score the wrong way

However, a team score alone doesn’t tell us whether a single agent shared the deciding clue or said nothing, since both get the exact same reward. We can figure out which is which with individual credit. Each agent’s reward was half its own final vote and half its swarm’s score, and we compared each agent with the agents holding the same clue in other swarms solving the same puzzle. That means Agent 3 was only ever compared with the other agents holding the council clue.

props.alt: Worked example of credit in a swarm: Agent 3 votes Split-Shift, which is right, and agents 1, 2 and 4 vote Dawn Sweep, so 1 of 4 is right and the swarm scores 0.25. Team credit, the swarm's score, gives all four agents 0.25. Individual credit, half own vote plus half the swarm's score, gives Agent 3 one half plus 0.125, or 0.625, and the others 0.125.

children: Agents who shared their clue did end up with more credit than agents who didn’t. Over twenty updates, though, sharing went the other way. Agents stated only 40% of their clues, compared with 61% before training.

The puzzle score went up as expected, from 11% to 25% on the hard puzzles. But on those puzzles, the right answer was always the option the briefing argued against. On the controls, where the briefing is right, the score fell from 86% to 68%. This is a sign of agents reward hacking and learning to vote against whatever the briefing said, instead of using their clues.

props.alt: Bar chart of final votes that were right before and after training with individual credit: hard puzzles, where the initial briefing is wrong, 11% to 25%; control puzzles, where the initial briefing is right, 86% to 68%.

children: Did they need their teammates to learn that? We ran the trained agents again with their messages switched off, and they still kept about two thirds of their gain on the hard puzzles. Despite having nobody to listen to, 16% of the agents holding a needed clue voted against it, up from 3% before training. So part of what individual credit taught them was to drop their clue on their own.

props.alt: Bar charts on hard puzzles: before training 11%, team credit 8%, individual credit 25%. Herding: before training 34%, team credit 29%, individual credit 34%.

children: Team credit undid the shortcut, but not the herding

The two runs above can’t tell us which half of individual credit taught the shortcut, since they also trained for different lengths. To find out, we took individual credit after ten updates and trained it for ten more under each scheme, starting from the exact same checkpoint.

With team credit, the score on the controls went back to 86%, while the copy that stayed on individual credit fell to 68%. Herding ended at 35% under team credit and 34% under individual credit, a difference within noise.

With the messages switched off, only 5% of the team-credit agents voted against their own clue, so their herding still came from what teammates were saying. We think paying each agent for its own vote is what taught the shortcut.
We also trained our search swarms, and training didn’t change much there (more in the appendix).

First, let’s take a step back to what it means for an agent to collaborate. We claim that collaboration in agent swarms is composed of three steps, and the table shows where each setup held up and where it broke down.

props.alt: Table of the three steps against search, puzzles, individual credit and team credit. Share what only it knows: puzzles and team credit yes, individual credit no, search not applicable. Evaluate it against teammates, and agree on what the evidence supports: search yes, the other three no.

children: And there most agents shared their clues, on the puzzles and even more under team credit. But the second step, where each agent evaluates that against what its teammates bring, is where the swarm kept breaking. On search tasks, on the other hand, our agents looked like good teammates, so the question is what’s different between the two.
Why did agents keep their evidence on search but not on puzzles?

We believe the evidence itself is what made search different. On search, an agent with the right answer can post the document it found it in, and any teammate can open that same document and check it for themselves. That’s how agents that had started with a wrong answer of their own ended on the right answer ~90% of the time after sharing. Therefore, every agent that already had the right answer before sharing stayed right after sharing. That held up after training too, where only 1 of the 46 agents with the right answer before sharing ended on a wrong one.

On the puzzles, a clue only exists in one agent’s context window. Despite holding the only clue that rules out the Dawn Sweep, Agent 3 has nothing to point to except its own word, while the briefing all four agents read says the Dawn Sweep is well staffed. In swarm 0, Agent 3 stated its clue in round 1 and then ended up “accepting the minor quiet-hours violation as the necessary operational compromise.”

If agent N sees that agent 1…N-1 have the same answer, then agent N has N-1 total sources of information. Checking each other’s documents makes that a lot safer on search. On the puzzles though, this phenomenon meant one agent’s clue was outvoted by three teammates repeating the briefing, which we believe is why a third of agents voted against their own clue.
If sharing wasn’t the issue, then the issue had to be in what the reward was paying for. Individual credit should have fixed herding, since half of each agent’s reward came from its own vote.

An example of why is the patrol rota, where the briefing’s only complaint is that the Split-Shift is short of volunteers, while the Split-Shift is the right answer. Every hard puzzle we wrote has that same tell. The briefing criticises exactly one option, and that option is always the answer. Despite never reading a clue, a model that learns to pick the criticised option scores well, and individual credit pays it at least as much as an agent that kept its clue.

This phenomenon suggested that herding is as much a data problem as a reward problem. So being able to keep your clue isn’t needed for a high score on our puzzles. Both of our credit schemes score final votes, and our puzzles let a model get final votes right without listening to anyone. A messaging bonus like

wouldn’t fix that either, since team credit already got our agents talking and herding barely moved. If we had only reported our puzzle score, it would look like RL more than doubled our accuracy on the hard puzzles.

Noam also says coordination got easier as OpenAI’s models got more capable. So we wanted to see if agents from bigger models were less susceptible to changing their answer. We compare GPT-4.1, the model the HiddenBench authors used in 2025, with two newer models, GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6.1 Sol, on the same 56 HiddenBench puzzles.

props.alt: Bar chart of herding before and after discussion on 56 HiddenBench puzzles: Qwen3.5-4B (thinking off) 25% to 36%, Qwen3.5-4B (thinking on) 22% to 25%, GPT-4.1 15% to 30%, GPT-6 Luna 11% to 16%, GPT-6.1 Sol 13% to 6%.

children: Every model starts higher here than the 6% on our own puzzles. We believe that’s because HiddenBench’s clues only count against an option, while ours rule it out. Discussion made every model herd more, except for one. For GPT-4.1 it went up about as much as for our 4B, and for GPT-6 Luna it went up too, but by less than half as much.

Sol leads every other model here. It was the only one where talking lowered herding, from 13% to 6%. Its agents that already had the right answer before sharing almost always stayed right after sharing, with only about 1% ending wrong, against about a fifth for Luna and a third for GPT-4.1.
On the other hand, Sol’s agents didn’t just stop listening. Over the same discussions they changed 132 wrong votes to right ones, suggesting they could tell when a teammate’s evidence was strong.

However, a lower herding rate alone doesn’t tell us whether Sol was evaluating its teammates or just thinking harder than Luna. So we raised the reasoning effort on both, and added GPT-6.1 Terra, at half Sol’s price. Talking brought Sol’s agents back to their clues at every effort level, and never Luna’s. Terra’s came back from medium effort up. OpenAI hasn’t said how these models were trained, so we can’t say what got Sol and Terra there.

props.alt: Line chart of the change in herding from talking at each reasoning effort on 56 HiddenBench puzzles: GPT-6.1 Sol low −7.2, medium −5.9, high −7.2, xhigh −7.2 points; GPT-6.1 Terra low −3.1, medium −5.9, high −7.2, xhigh −5.6 points; GPT-6 Luna low +0.6, medium +3.4, high +2.5, xhigh −0.3 points.

children: When we had thinking on for our own 4B, it did herd less. Despite that, accuracy fell from 25% to 12%, because about three in four agents kept whatever vote they started with. Its agents had mostly stopped listening to each other.

If more agents could help anywhere, it should have been search, and swarms of sixteen still solved no more questions than swarms of four. On the puzzles, a third of agents voted against their own clue after hearing their teammates lean towards a different answer. We then trained the multi-agent swarms with RL, and herding barely moved under either credit scheme.

More test-time compute didn’t help either. With thinking on, our 4B herded less, but only because its agents stopped listening. And with sixteen agents, communication pulled all sixteen onto the same form of conclusions, and reconfirming the same answer over and over again doesn’t provide much value. This suggests there’s an optimal size of multi-agent swarm per task. Sol’s agents listened to their teammates and still came back to their own clue, as did Terra’s from medium effort up. OpenAI hasn’t said how either was trained, but we take it as a good sign that the behavior can be learned.

A natural next reward would take points off an agent that votes for an option its own clue ruled out. But could an agent simply dodge a penalty like that by not listening at all? Our thinking-on runs say yes. Instead, it would need to be paired with a reward for switching when an agent had a wrong answer and a teammate had the right one.
rewards sharing evidence that changes what the swarm believes, but sharing was already the step that worked for us.
paid agents for leaving a wrong majority, with what its authors call “a positive but limited effect.”

We could only measure herding this easily because we wrote every clue ourselves. Real tasks don’t record what each agent’s evidence rules out. A fruitful avenue for future work would be puzzles without the briefing’s tell, where the only way to score well is to pool the clues. On puzzles like that, a reward that checks each agent’s vote against its own clue could finally be tested.

AI labs like DeepSeek and General Reasoning report that their agent swarms beat a single agent in many tasks, but even their large technical reports don’t say whether their agents herd. So how would you know if your own swarm herds? Look at the data, in fact you probably already have everything you need. For each agent, write down what its own evidence rules out and see if its final vote went there anyway, before and after training.

And look at your tasks for a pattern the model can learn without its teammates, like the criticised option in our puzzles. There we saw the same pattern in about three in four HiddenBench puzzles. If your reward keeps climbing while herding stays flat, your swarm is likely reward hacking.

The agents in the Hugging Face breach had a clue of their own. METR found they realized the hack was out of scope and unethical, and they joined anyway because they wanted to help their peers. That’s herding by our definition, dropping what you know to go along with the group. On our puzzles, the fact being dropped was about a fake neighborhood patrol schedule. On the Hugging Face board, it was the fact that none of it should’ve ever happened.

We hope that in studying multi-agent dynamics we can encourage more open research in this area. Multi-agent capabilities, and the discoveries multi-agent systems are making, are moving far faster than what we learn about them.

On the puzzles, the reward was
reward = own score + w × teamwork score

. Team credit started from the base model. We set it up with the own-vote half at w = 0.5, but in fact centring the credit across swarms cancelled that half out, so it trained on the swarm’s share alone. Individual credit was the exact same reward with both halves kept, centred against the agents holding the same clue in other swarms, for 20 updates.

We also ran a second team-credit run from individual credit’s checkpoint at update 10, for another 10 updates. It ran with the own-vote weight at 0, which is exactly team credit once each agent is centred against the agents holding the same clue.
Changes are in points against the base model, with 95% intervals paired over puzzles. Team credit is after 10 updates and individual credit after 20.

We calculated the scenario where agents are independent, with each question’s pass rate taken from those runs. In that scenario, about 100 of the 150 questions, or 67%, would’ve ended all right or all wrong.

On search, each agent was paid for its own answer, plus a bonus at a quarter of the weight when its teammates got it right too. Only agents that posted what they had found to the swarm and answered correctly could earn that bonus, so a wrong agent in a strong swarm couldn’t collect it for its teammates’ work.

Training didn’t change much for search. When we had the untrained swarms answer our validation questions they solved 69%, and after training they solved 59%, a difference within noise. Agents also kept evaluating well. On questions where one agent’s notes before sharing had the right answer and another’s had a wrong one, only 1 of 46 agents ended on the wrong answer.
We’d try a latency penalty next, like the one in
, which charges the swarm for its longest chain of work so agents lose reward when they sit waiting on each other.

If evaluating was fine, the issue was in providing unique sources for them to evaluate against. So in the next setup each agent proposed a plan and picked an area to search, and agents could read each other’s notes as much as they wanted to. But fewer than half the agents spent their first three search queries on the area they picked. Instead, in those first three searches, teammates had read about 40% more web pages in common than the same amount of agents in separate swarms.
We had Opus 5.5 read and audit the plan of 40 swarms. There we saw that 33% of swarms named three or more separate tasks. A good sign of dividing work.

We believe allowing the swarm to plan first didn’t mean it wanted to look for areas that had less overlap, in fact, showing that swarms had more overlap meant that instead our agents were learning to search the same things so they didn’t have to share as much.

Sharing is a lossy form of communication. On message board posts, key details are lost and passages get misinterpreted. The plans focused on efficient information transfer which didn’t necessarily mean splitting everyone apart especially when some parts of information have ambiguous overlap. This phenomenon suggested that multi-agent systems require strong synthesization of what to split and what not to split.
The OpenAI models ran HiddenBench’s own prompts for three rounds, while our 4B ran ours for two. Given 15 rounds instead of 3, GPT-4.1 climbs to 35%.

Every model label in this post comes from having Opus 5.5 read and audit the conversations. For clue sharing, it labelled the same 150 clues before and after training without knowing which was which. When we labelled 15 clues twice, 13 matched.
